newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Imelda Marcos demands hero's burial for husband.
newsitem.headline: Imelda Marcos demands hero's burial for husband.

text.p: Former Philippine first lady Imelda Marcos on Wednesday demanded a hero's burial for her late husband, Ferdinand, and said President Fidel Ramos had agreed to it in writing as part of a political deal.
Ramos, now touring south Asia, said on Tuesday the Marcos family was free to bury the former president anywhere in Manila but not at a state cemetery reserved for heroes.
The row over where Marcos is to be buried erupted after a power firm on Monday cut the electricity to his mausoleum in his hometown of Batac in a dispute over unpaid electricity bills.
Batac mayor Jesus Nalupta Power said he was getting a second-hand generator to restore power to the mausoleum later on Wednesday.

Mrs. Marcos told reporters that Ramos signed the agreement with her "when he was wooing my support" prior to his proclamation as president after bitterly contested elections in which she also ran and lost.
She said Ramos promised in writing that after he took office, "he will allow the honourable burial of my husband" at the Heroes Cemetery for soldiers.
"He even signed the covenant in red ink," said Mrs. Marcos, now a member of the Congress.

Marcos was ousted in a popular revolt in 1986 and accused of plundering the Philippine economy. His personal biographers said he won about 30 medals for heroism in World War Two but some historians dispute this.
Mrs. Marcos said her husband deserved to be buried at the Heroes Cemetery because he was "a soldier of the Republic."
"He will lie wherever he deserves to rest in peace for always," she told Reuters.

The former president died in exile in Hawaii in 1989. Ramos allowed his remains to be brought to Batac, in the northern Philippines, in 1993 but refused then to allow his burial in Manila, fearing it would provoke violence.
Since then the corpse has lain in an elevated glass coffin in the air-conditioned mausoleum in the family backyard. Embalmers injected it with chemicals that they said would preserve it for 10 years.
Up until power was cut on Monday, the wax-like cadaver had been bathed in soft lights 24 hours a day while music by Mozart and other classical masters played in the background.
"I just talked to the former first lady and I told her that I will be bringing a generator today to give power to the mausoleum and the water pump," Nalupta told Reuters.
"The generator will come any time today, so power will be restored today," he said.
"It is an old one," he added.
